mcqs.question: An export endpoint builds a job id, pushes `{ jobId, body }` onto an in-process array, and answers `202` with `{ jobId, statusUrl }`. A rolling deploy restarts the process one second later, before any worker has picked the job up. The client polls the `statusUrl` it was given. What does it get, and what was the actual defect?
options: Nothing the client can notice: `202` is noncommittal, so a server may drop the accepted work at any time.
A `500` from the status endpoint, because the job row it looks up does not exist after the restart.
A permanent `404`: the response handed out a status monitor, so the record had to be durable before the `202` left.
A job stuck in `pending`: the row survives, but the queue entry that would have run it is gone.
mcqs.explanation: The `202` and the `statusUrl` are one promise: the client is told which resource to watch, so that resource has to exist by the time the response is sent, because a crash between the response and a durable write is not something the client can recover from. Nothing in the snippet stores the job anywhere outside process memory, so every later poll asks for an id that was never written and gets `404`. The strongest distractor is the noncommittal reading: RFC 9110 does call `202` noncommittal, but about whether the processing eventually happens, not about forgetting the id it just published; the fix is to persist the job before answering, then let a worker pick it up from the record. The `500` option confuses 'this id does not exist' with 'the status service itself is broken', and the `pending` option assumes a row the code never writes.

mcqs.question: Two concurrent retries of `POST /payments` reach the service after a client timeout. Which change actually makes the duplicate charge impossible, rather than merely unlikely?
options: Generate the idempotency key on the server at the start of each attempt, so every attempt is traceable.
Have the client send one key per intent, and write the payment plus that key in one transaction under a unique constraint.
`SELECT` the key before inserting the payment, and skip the insert when a row is already there.
Hash the body on the server and merge two identical payments that arrive inside the same minute.
mcqs.explanation: Only the client knows which attempts are retries of one intent, so the key has to come from the client and stay identical across them; the server then makes the race safe with a unique constraint on the key and commits the payment and its key in one transaction, so neither exists without the other. The strongest distractor is the `SELECT` guard: it looks like the same lookup a correct design does, but placed before the insert it is check-then-act, so two concurrent attempts both read nothing and both insert, and a crash between the two writes leaves a payment with no key at all; the constraint, not the read, is what serializes them. A server-generated key is different on every attempt, which makes the duplicate look like a brand-new intent. Hashing the body collapses two legitimate identical payments into a silent loss and still misses duplicates outside the window.

mcqs.question: A stream worker calls `XACK` for an entry and only then runs the business handler. The process is killed between the two. What happened to that entry, and what ordering do you want?
options: It is still pending, so `XAUTOCLAIM` hands it to a live consumer once its idle time passes the threshold.
It left the pending list, so the work is lost: ack after the side effect, and make the handler idempotent for the other window.
It keeps its delivery count, so the next `>` read from a live consumer returns it for another attempt.
`XACK` also removed it from the stream, so there is nothing left for any consumer to replay.
mcqs.explanation: `XACK` is the operation that takes an entry off the group's pending list, and that list is the only surface from which an unprocessed entry can be recovered: acking first records the work as done before it is done, so no recovery path can see it. Acking after the side effect closes that loss window and opens the duplicate window instead, which is exactly why the handler itself has to be idempotent rather than trusting the ordering alone. The strongest distractor is `XAUTOCLAIM`: it scans the group's pending entries by idle time, so an entry that was already acknowledged is simply not there to claim, and the `>` option repeats the error, because `>` only delivers entries never delivered to the group. `XACK` never deletes stream data; trimming is a separate `XADD MAXLEN` or `XTRIM` decision.

mcqs.question: A webhook worker gets `404 Not Found` from a merchant endpoint on the first delivery attempt. What is the correct reaction in a pipeline built on an outbox plus per-destination retries?
options: Treat it as delivered, because the endpoint answered with an HTTP status code.
Stop retrying, record the attempt as a permanent failure, and route it to the dead-letter path while surfacing the broken endpoint to the merchant.
Retry with exponential backoff up to the attempt cap, then dead-letter whatever is left.
Retry immediately in a tight loop, because the first failure of a 4xx is usually transient.
mcqs.explanation: A 404 says the target does not exist, so no amount of backoff will make it succeed: retrying only delays the alert and hides a broken integration behind hours of scheduled attempts. The pipeline should classify per status code, because 408, 425 and 429 are 4xx yet retryable exceptions (with `Retry-After` honored), not treat the whole 4xx class as one thing. The strongest distractor is retrying until the cap and then dead-lettering: it sounds prudent and eventually parks the message, but it spends the full retry budget on an error that is known permanent, so both the merchant's fix and your own detection arrive late.

mcqs.question: A pod receives `SIGTERM` while the load balancer is still routing to it. Which shutdown order actually avoids dropping in-flight requests?
options: Mark the instance unready, wait for routing to stop reaching it, then stop accepting new connections and drain in-flight work up to a bounded deadline.
Drain in-flight requests first, then mark the instance unready, then exit, because readiness only affects pods that have not started yet.
Close the listener immediately so no new connection is half-accepted, then mark unready and drain.
Exit as soon as `SIGTERM` arrives; the orchestrator replays interrupted requests against another replica.
mcqs.explanation: Removal from load-balancer or Service endpoints is asynchronous, so the instance keeps receiving traffic after the signal; becoming unready first, then pausing long enough for routing to catch up, is what makes the drain finite. Only then can the listener close while existing connections finish, with a hard deadline so one stuck dependency cannot block the rollout. The strongest distractor is draining before going unready: the drain never converges, because new requests keep arriving while the instance is still considered healthy, and the only thing left is the deadline cutting them off.

mcqs.question: A scheduler reads due schedule rows, enqueues one job per row, and only afterwards advances `nextRun` in a separate transaction. Which failure does that ordering leave open?
options: Nothing serious: the queue deduplicates by job type, so a re-emitted occurrence is harmless.
A crash between the advance and the enqueue loses the occurrence, so the fix is to advance before enqueueing.
A crash after the enqueue but before the advance re-emits the same occurrence on the next tick; the fix is a per-occurrence idempotency key plus an atomic or conditional advance.
The scheduler should execute the job itself, so enqueue and execution become a single step and no window exists.
mcqs.explanation: Enqueue-then-advance is the right direction, but the two writes are not one unit, so a crash in between leaves `nextRun` in the past and the same occurrence is emitted again. That is why the emitted command carries a key derived from the schedule and its occurrence (`id:nextRun` in the bank's example), and why the advance must be atomic or conditional so two schedulers cannot both claim it. The strongest distractor is reversing the order: advancing first closes the duplicate window by opening a loss window instead, which is the worse failure for a billing or reminder job. Deduplicating by job type is wrong too, since it would collapse genuinely distinct runs of the same job.

scenarios.prompt: Support keeps seeing duplicate payments whenever a client times out on `POST /payments` and retries with the same idempotency key. Walk through what this handler does under that retry, name every window that can produce a second charge, and give the design that closes them. Say what happens when the same key arrives with a different payload, and how long the key lives.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
The handler is a check-then-act with its two writes split, so there are three separate ways to charge twice.

**Window 1: the payment exists, the key does not.** `db.payment.create` and `db.idempotency.create` are separate statements. A deploy, a dropped connection or a process kill between them leaves a real payment with no idempotency record; the retry calls `findUnique`, gets `null`, charges again and writes a fresh key row. The fix is one transaction that writes the payment and the key together, so the key exists if and only if the payment exists.

**Window 2: two attempts read `null` together.** `findUnique` returning nothing is not a reservation. The original request and its retry can both be in flight - a client double submit, a proxy replay, a retry issued before the first attempt died - and both read `null` before either writes. Only a `UNIQUE` constraint on the key serializes them: one insert wins, the other violates the constraint, and the loser must read the row and replay the stored response instead of returning an error. `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on its own is not enough; the handler still has to read the row and decide between replay and conflict.

**Window 3: the retry lands while the first attempt is still running.** `return existing.response` assumes a response was already stored. Store a state with the key - in progress, succeeded, failed - and answer `409 Conflict` for in-progress, so the client backs off instead of starting a second payment. A key row with no state forces the handler to guess which attempt arrived first.

On the two decisions the prompt asks for. A reused key carrying a different payload is a client bug, not a retry: hash the canonical request, compare it against the stored hash, and answer `409` or `422`, because applying the new payload silently turns an accidental reuse into a mutation. Retention has to outlive every retry the client is allowed to make, including retries queued behind an outage - hours to a day is an honest range for a payments API - and the key has to be scoped, by merchant or account, so two clients cannot collide on the same string. Past the window the guarantee ends and the same key means a new intent.

Finally, none of this makes the provider idempotent: send the same key with the charge request, or the local rows can be perfect while the card is charged twice.
rubric: Traces the retry through the snippet: `findUnique` returns `null`, so the second charge comes from the handler rather than from the client.
Names the split write: a crash between the payment insert and the key insert leaves a payment no retry can see, and both writes must commit together.
Explains why `findUnique` is not a reservation and that the unique constraint, not the read, settles concurrent retries, with the loser replaying the stored response.
Adds a key state so an in-progress attempt answers `409`, and rejects a reused key whose request hash differs.
Scopes and expires the key on a documented window and passes it to the payment provider so the downstream charge is idempotent too.

scenarios.prompt: A worker consumes Redis Streams messages and occasionally crashes. On-call reports two symptoms: entries that were being processed at crash time are never processed again, and a freshly restarted worker pins a CPU core while the stream is empty. Review the code, explain both symptoms, and give a safe processing loop with recovery and the metrics you would alarm on.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Ack-after-effect is already the right order, so neither symptom comes from it. Keep it, and put the idempotency somewhere else.

**Symptom 1: the dead worker's entries are stranded.** Everything this worker read is in the group's pending entries list, and nothing in the code ever looks there again. `>` means entries never delivered to the group, so the restarted worker does not see them and no other replica does either; they sit in the PEL forever while the group reports them as pending. The recovery loop is a periodic `XPENDING jobs workers - + 100` to see what is stuck, then `XAUTOCLAIM jobs workers 60000 0-0 COUNT 10` to take ownership of entries idle past the threshold, process them and ack them. The min-idle time has to be longer than p99 processing time, or a worker that is merely slow gets its entry stolen and both handlers run. Every claim increments the delivery count, which is also the attempt counter the retry policy should read.

**Symptom 2: CPU burn on an empty stream.** `XREADGROUP` without `BLOCK` returns immediately when there is nothing new, `poll()` falls through the empty loop, and whatever calls it again spins. Read with `BLOCK 5000` and a client timeout longer than the block, so the loop waits for data instead of polling, and keep a short sleep on the error path.

Two more things are wrong with the loop rather than with the ordering. The consumer name is the constant `alice`, so every replica registers as the same consumer: the group cannot tell instances apart, per-consumer pending counts are meaningless, and a restart that resumes its own pending entries with id `0` would hand the same entries to every replica at once. Use the pod or process id, and read `0` once at start to finish what that instance left behind.

There is also no per-entry error handling. One throwing entry aborts the batch, and the entries after it were already delivered, so they stay pending without ever being retried. Wrap each entry, count attempts, retry transient failures with backoff, and after N attempts write the payload and the last error to a dead-letter stream or quarantine table, acking only after that write, so a poison entry stops clogging the PEL.

Retention has to outlive the repair window. Trim with a window longer than the recovery SLA, because an entry that is trimmed before anyone claims it is dropped from the PEL by the next claim attempt and the work is gone for good.

Metrics: `XINFO GROUPS` for lag, pending count and last-delivered-id; age of the oldest pending entry; delivery counts above one; processing latency; dead-letter depth; claim rate. Alarm on pending age rather than on pending count, because a steady count with a young age is a busy group, not a broken one.
rubric: Keeps ack-after-effect and adds idempotency in `doBusinessChange`, separating the duplicate window from the loss window.
Identifies that `>` never redelivers the dead consumer's entries and adds a recovery loop over the PEL with `XPENDING` and `XAUTOCLAIM` and a min-idle threshold.
Replaces the constant `alice` consumer name with a per-instance identity and resumes that instance's own pending entries with id `0` on start.
Explains the missing `BLOCK` as the cause of the CPU spin and adds per-entry error handling with bounded retries and a dead-letter path acked after the park write.
Bounds stream length above the recovery SLA and names the metrics to alarm on: lag, pending age, delivery count, dead-letter depth.

scenarios.prompt: This is the outbound webhook path of an orders service. Review it as if you owned the integration: find the durability, signing, retry and ordering defects, then redesign the pipeline (outbox, retries, dead letters) and state the delivery contract you would publish to merchants.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
The handler couples the merchant's availability to the checkout path and gives up durability to do it: the order is committed, then the fetch happens inside the same request, so a crash or deploy between the two loses the event forever, and a slow endpoint holds a request worker open. The retry is also unusable as written — unbounded recursion with no delay, no attempt cap, no classification, and a stack that grows while the caller waits — and re-signing only the body with a long-lived secret means a captured request can be replayed indefinitely, with no event id for the receiver to deduplicate on.

I would rebuild it in four stages. First, a transactional outbox: the business update and an outbox row (event id, type, aggregate id, payload, merchant id, created at) commit in one transaction, so the event exists if and only if the state change exists. Second, a relay that reads undispatched outbox rows and publishes them to a durable per-destination queue or stream, marking rows dispatched idempotently; the queue key is the destination plus the aggregate id, so deliveries for one merchant's orders stay ordered while unrelated traffic stays parallel. Third, a delivery worker per endpoint: it loads the attempt record, signs the exact bytes it will send as `HMAC(secret, timestamp + '.' + rawBody)`, adds the key id, timestamp and event id headers, and posts once. Retryable outcomes — timeouts, connection resets, 408, 425, 429 (honoring `Retry-After`) and 5xx — get bounded exponential backoff with jitter; permanent ones such as 400, 401, 403, 404, 410 and 422 stop immediately. Fourth, when the attempt budget or the delivery window is exhausted, the attempt moves to a dead-letter store with payload, target, attempt count and last status or error; DLQ depth and age are alerted, and replay is an audited operation that re-enqueues the same event id with a fresh budget so receiver-side dedupe still holds.

The published contract is at-least-once, not exactly-once: receivers must deduplicate on the event id, verify the signature over the timestamp plus raw body and reject stale timestamps, tolerate out-of-order arrival across aggregates, and rotate secrets with overlapping key ids. Operationally I would expose delivery latency, per-endpoint success rate, attempt distribution, DLQ depth and age, and outbox lag, because a merchant silently failing for a day is the failure this design is meant to make visible. Kubernetes' pod termination flow and Stripe's documented retry behavior are the reference points for the drain and backoff semantics (https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination-flow, https://docs.stripe.com/webhooks#automatic-retries).

What I would not claim is zero loss on the merchant side: with at-least-once delivery and a third party we control neither, the honest guarantee is durable emission, bounded retries, a visible dead-letter path and a replay story.
rubric: Names the missing transactional outbox: the event can be lost between the committed order and the fetch, and merchant latency is coupled to the request path.
Corrects the signing contract: HMAC over timestamp plus the exact bytes sent, plus an event id so receivers can deduplicate.
Replaces the recursive retry with bounded exponential backoff, jitter and per-status classification (retry timeouts/408/429/5xx, stop on permanent 4xx, honor `Retry-After`).
Defines a dead-letter path with payload and attempt metadata, alerting on depth and age, and an audited replay that preserves the event id.
Scopes ordering to destination plus aggregate, keeps unrelated traffic parallel, and publishes the at-least-once contract with receiver-side obligations.
